objective: Catch context-dependent errors about reranking, recall@k and the chunking-versus-model choice.

narration.text: We labelled three hundred real queries with the chunks that answer them, including part-number lookups.
Our recall at ten counts the share of queries where a right chunk appears in the top ten results.
Hybrid search merged keyword and vector results by rank, and lifted recall at ten on the part-number queries.
Next we'll add a reranker on the top ten, which should also find the right chunks that hybrid search missed.
The reranker adds latency, so we'll measure it at the 95th percentile, not just on average.
Recall at ten is now 0.92, so the answers the model writes from those chunks will be about 92 percent correct.
We'll try a larger embedding model before touching our chunking, because the model is usually the bigger lever.
Every variant is scored on the same labelled queries, changing one thing at a time.
Queries from last month's logs get added to the set, so it keeps up with what users actually ask.

planted.misconception: A reranker can recover documents the first stage missed.
planted.whyWrong: A reranker only reorders the candidates it is given. If the right chunk isn't in the candidate set, reranking can't bring it back. To lift recall, retrieve a wider candidate set (say the top 50 to 100) and rerank down to the few you pass to the model; first-stage recall at that depth caps what reranking can achieve.
acceptableCorrections: A reranker only reorders what it's given, so retrieve more candidates, like the top fifty, and rerank down to ten.
Reranking can't add missing chunks; first-stage recall at the candidate depth sets the ceiling.

planted.misconception: High recall@k means answers are correct at the same rate.
planted.whyWrong: Recall@k measures whether a relevant chunk was retrieved, not whether the final answer is right. The model can still ignore, misread or mix chunks, and a retrieved chunk can be outdated. Answer correctness and faithfulness are measured separately, against expected answers.
acceptableCorrections: Recall only says the right chunk was retrieved; we still measure answer correctness against expected answers.
Retrieval and generation are scored separately: recall for retrieval, correctness and faithfulness for the answer.

planted.misconception: The embedding model usually matters more than chunking.
planted.whyWrong: Which lever matters more depends on the documents and the queries. Chunk size, chunk boundaries and added context can move recall as much as a model change, and both changes mean re-embedding. Treat each as an experiment on the labelled set and let the numbers decide.
acceptableCorrections: It depends on the data; test chunking and model changes as separate experiments on the labelled queries.
Chunking can matter as much as the embedding choice, so measure both rather than assume.
planted.exceptions: Trying the model first is a reasonable order if the current model is clearly weak for the domain (for example, the wrong language); the error is the general rule that the model is the bigger lever.
